subject: Evaluating uplink handshake: Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN (AcmeBridge)
messages:
From: Mike Chen <mike.chen@acmebridge.io>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi@redwood.com>
Cc: AcmeBridge Networking <networking@acmebridge.io>
Date: Mon, 26 Apr 2027 16:12:00 -0400
Subject: Onramp options for private deployment (short ask)

Hi Naomi,

Thanks for taking a look at our private deployment plans. We're standing up a small on-prem inference cluster (pilot) and evaluating how best to connect to Redwood Private in the cloud. Our primary goals: minimal latency for inference calls, strict egress control for PHI, and straightforward operational ownership for NetOps.

High-level constraints:
- We cannot open broad egress from on-prem; traffic must be tightly scoped.
- We prefer managed endpoints over heavy NAT-ing if possible.
- Expected traffic for pilot: ~200 r/s with bursts to 800 r/s during load tests.

Can you summarize the practical tradeoffs between VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN for this use case? Also attaching a simple network diagram.

Attachment: acmebridge-onprem-network-diagram.pdf (PDF, 420KB)

--
Mike Chen
Platform Architect, AcmeBridge
mike.chen@acmebridge.io
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi@redwood.com>
To: Mike Chen <mike.chen@acmebridge.io>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 26 Apr 2027 18:04:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Onramp options for private deployment (short ask)

Mike — thanks for the clear constraints and the diagram. I pulled Ben (infra) and Kimberly (security) in so we can give an operational answer rather than a textbook list. Below is a concise comparative view and a recommended next step.

Quick summary (short):
- VPC peering: Lowest network hop latency inside the cloud, but only useful if the on-prem connects through a cloud VPC (e.g., via transit/colocation). Peering does not traverse the public internet and is good for high-throughput, low-latency flows between cloud VPCs. Does not provide a managed ingress surface for on-prem to reach Redwood Private directly.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): Managed, private-by-default; allows your on-prem to reach Redwood service using interface endpoints and endpoint network interfaces in your VPC. Strong isolation and easy service-level access control; easier for NetOps to reason about. Slightly more operational overhead to manage endpoint IPs/security groups.
- Site-to-site VPN: Fastest to stand up from a project timeline perspective; can be encrypted and controlled. Performance depends on your VPN appliance and ISP; latency/jitter can be variable. Requires careful routing/NAT planning and doesn't provide the same per-service access controls as PrivateLink.

Recommendation for pilot: PrivateLink-backed ingress with a short-lived S2S VPN as a fallback for initial traffic cuts. PrivateLink meets your egress-control and isolation needs while giving predictable AWS-native routing. We can advise on required security groups and recommended MTU settings.

Next step: Can we do a 45-minute tech sync Wednesday? Ben can run a short throughput/latency sketch and Kimberly will note audit/logging guardrails.

Thanks,
Naomi
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference
naomi@redwood.com

Adding engineering details from the serving/runtime perspective.

Ben here — short bullet list of operational differences you should plan for:

- Latency: VPC peering (cloud-to-cloud) typically has lowest intra-cloud latency. PrivateLink adds ~1-3 ms overhead because traffic goes through ENIs and NLBs (if used). S2S VPN will vary; expect +10-50 ms depending on circuit and public path. For your 200–800 r/s burst, PrivateLink is still well within acceptable tail latency for most workloads if you keep packet/frame sizes small and enable TCP keepalives.
- Throughput & scaling: PrivateLink scales horizontally by adding more ENIs/NLB capacity; however, it requires coordination (we recommend autoscaling at the service edge). If you plan sustained thousands of r/s eventually, discuss dedicated capacity (Redwood Dedicated) or burst policies.
- Failover: If your on-prem ISP hiccups, VPN will failover quickly only if you have redundant tunnels and dynamic routing (BGP). PrivateLink combined with multi-region endpoint configurations and routing policies provides higher reliability overall with less operational churn.
- Observability: PrivateLink lets us tie requests to endpoint ENIs for audit logs; VPNs need packet capture/process-level logging on your appliance for the same fidelity (harder).
- NAT/Porting: Avoid double-NAT — ensure the on-prem -> transit -> VPC path preserves source IPs or use x-forwarded-for semantics for request attribution.

Operational tip: For the pilot, implement a short time-window A/B: route 80% of traffic over PrivateLink and hold 20% on S2S to validate performance under load. We can provide config snippets for iperf and curl-based synthetic checks.

--
Ben Carter
Sr. Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference
ben@redwood.com
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>

Date: Wed, 28 Apr 2027 13:03:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Onramp options for private deployment (short ask)

Mike — adding a few compliance and audit items you should bake into your plan:

- Data egress controls: PrivateLink gives you a well-scoped ingress surface. That makes applying egress deny-by-default rules simpler on your edge. If you use VPN, ensure your firewall rules explicitly only allow traffic to Redwood service ranges and log denies to a SIEM.
- Key management & TLS: Use mTLS between your on-prem clients and Redwood if you need mutual authentication. We support customer-managed keys in our Private setup; ask if you'd like a KMS/HSM diagram.
- Auditability: Request-level tracing (request IDs) must be injected at the client and preserved by the gateway. PrivateLink + our tracing headers gives cleaner chain-of-custody; VPNs require extra instrumentation.
- Cert rotation & revocation: If you plan to share client certs across appliances, ensure you have a revocation plan (CRL/OCSP) — we can automate short-lived cert issuance for pilot services.

I'm fine with the suggested ramp: PrivateLink primary; VPN fallback for the initial cutover window. Mike, if you can share the exact appliance model and bandwidth over the weekend I'll draft a short ops checklist with MTU, BGP hints (if applicable), and firewall rules.

Kimberly Park
Director, Security & Compliance — Redwood Inference
